section_summary: This section documents the severe political and financial crisis in Japan in early 1937, marked by growing public and parliamentary opposition to the military's budget demands and political dominance. It covers the collapse of the Hirota Cabinet following heated attacks in the Diet, the Army's veto of General Kazunari Ugaki's attempt to form a government, and the installation of General Senjuro Hayashi's cabinet. Detailed reporting highlights financial strain from military spending, the appointment of Naotake Sato as Foreign Minister, Hayashi's vague five-point policy statement, and Kwantung Army efforts to establish a totalitarian single-party political structure.

subfiles.about: Concluding pages of Ambassador Grew's annual survey examining Japan's economic difficulties, mounting deficit bond issues, and financial strains resulting from military expenditures.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This concluding portion of Despatch No. 2209 evaluates Japan's economic and financial stability at the start of 1937. It notes that heavy military spending and arms replenishment programs are driving inflation, increasing commodity prices, and threatening a serious adverse balance of trade. The Government faces mounting difficulties in marketing 3.5% deficit bonds to the public and maintaining the exchange value of the yen at one shilling two pence. Ambassador Grew suggests that artificial exchange controls and import restrictions similar to those in Germany will likely be required to prevent a severe financial crisis.
subfiles.title: General Situation Facing Japan at the Opening of the Year 1937 (Conclusion)

subfiles.about: State Department analysis of Ambassador Grew's annual survey, arguing that the despatch is overly pessimistic regarding Japanese foreign policy and domestic conditions.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: The memorandum summarizes Ambassador Grew's Despatch No. 2209 covering Japan's foreign relations, domestic politics, military role, and economic status. Far Eastern Division analysts offer a critical commentary arguing that Grew's depiction is excessively pessimistic and fails to give sufficient weight to counterbalancing moderate factors. They point out that recent Japanese statements disclaim naval competition and note that the Army, while entrenched, appears sobered by public dissatisfaction and mounting international obstacles.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Ambassador Grew's Despatch No. 2209 Regarding the General Situation Facing Japan

subfiles.about: Brief State Department note noting that political, economic, and financial conditions in Japan have improved since the drafting of Despatch No. 2209.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: This brief internal note asserts that developments since January 1, 1937 have changed the domestic political and economic landscape. It concludes that contemporary conditions in international relations, domestic politics, and finance are not as unfavorable as depicted when Despatch No. 2209 was prepared.
subfiles.title: Note on Recent Developments in Japan Since Despatch No. 2209

subfiles.about: State Department summary and commentary on Despatch No. 2241 detailing seven rebuffs suffered by the Japanese Army during January 1937.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (JP), Department of State
subfiles.summary: The memorandum summarizes the main points of Despatch No. 2241 concerning political tensions in Japan during January 1937. It emphasizes seven setbacks experienced by the Army despite its successful prevention of an anti-military Premier. The commentary notes that Premier Hayashi's moderate stance reflects the precarious balance between radical military reformers and civilian elements alarmed by military socioeconomic doctrine.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Despatch No. 2241: Political Developments in Japan, January 1937
subfiles.to: Wallace T. Treadwell, Eugene H. Dooman, and Maxwell M. Hamilton

subfiles.about: Detailed report on the Japanese political crisis of January 1937, the fall of the Hirota Cabinet, the blocking of General Ugaki, and the appointment of General Hayashi.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew (signed by Cabot Coville), American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 2241 chronicles the political upheaval ignited by Kunimatsu Hamada's aggressive interpellation in the Diet on January 21, 1937, attacking military interference in civil government. Following the dissolution dispute and the subsequent resignation of the Hirota Cabinet, the Army blocked General Kazunari Ugaki from forming a ministry by refusing to appoint a War Minister, prompting Ugaki to release an explosive statement condemning military meddling. The Embassy outlines seven specific rebuffs experienced by the Army during this sequence and evaluates General Senjuro Hayashi's appointment as a fragile compromise between military factions and civilian business interests.
subfiles.title: Political Developments in Japan, January 1937 (Despatch No. 2241)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a memorandum on political developments in Japan, the appointment of General Sugiyama as War Minister, and Premier Hayashi's program.
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: This document file note records a memorandum by John Carter Vincent regarding the situation in Japan during early February 1937. It indexes reporting on the appointment of General Gen Sugiyama as Minister of War and provides an interpretation of Premier Hayashi's policy statement announced on February 8.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: The Situation in the Far East: Japan (894.00/698)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a memorandum on developments in China during the preceding week.
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes a memorandum by John Carter Vincent concerning weekly developments in China. The underlying document is cross-referenced under file number 893.00/14020.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: The Situation in the Far East: China (894.00/699)

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting the appointment and press reception of Naotake Sato as Japan's Minister for Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 69 reports the installation of Naotake Sato, former Ambassador to France, as Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs. Ambassador Grew summarizes Sato's career, his public statements emphasizing foreign policy continuity, and his anticipation of friction with the service ministers. Tokyo press commentary generally welcomed Sato's career diplomatic experience while highlighting the necessity of coordinating policy between the Foreign Office, Army, and Navy.
subfiles.title: Appointment of Naotake Sato as Minister for Foreign Affairs (Telegram No. 69)

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum evaluating Despatch No. 2256 on the Hayashi Cabinet's statement of policy.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (WTT), Department of State
subfiles.summary: This Far Eastern Division memorandum reviews Embassy Tokyo's Despatch No. 2256 analyzing Premier Hayashi's five-point platform. The analyst cautions against reading too much into the vague phrasing of the document, specifically questioning the Embassy's conclusion that Japan had openly declared its armaments to be intended for national expansion.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Despatch No. 2256: Policies of the Hayashi Cabinet

subfiles.about: Embassy report analyzing the five-point policy statement issued by the Hayashi Cabinet, accompanied by a newspaper clipping of the Premier's radio address.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 2256 reviews the five-point policy platform published by Premier Hayashi on February 8, 1937, written in archaic classical Japanese. The Embassy translates and scrutinizes each principle, identifying implicit warnings against party dominance, signs of a desire to move away from secret diplomacy, an open declaration that armaments serve external expansion, and contradictions regarding state economic control. An attached clipping from The Japan Advertiser of February 12, 1937, provides the English text of Hayashi's Empire Day radio address reiterating these principles.
subfiles.title: Policies of the Hayashi Cabinet (Despatch No. 2256)

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum reviewing Despatch No. 2273 on the formation of a rightist, Army-inspired monopoly political party.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (JB), Department of State
subfiles.summary: This memorandum analyzes Embassy Tokyo's reporting on an emerging rightist political party initiated by Army circles. The analyst observes that while this movement shares fascist opposition to democratic institutions and seeks a monopoly of power, political loyalties in Japan depend more heavily on personal leadership than on formal ideological platforms.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Despatch No. 2273: New Party Movement in Japan

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum commenting on Despatch No. 2268 concerning the formation of the Hayashi Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (JB), Department of State
subfiles.summary: This memorandum discusses Tokyo Despatch No. 2268 regarding the background of General Hayashi's selection as a compromise Premier. The analysis suggests that placing a military officer directly at the head of government leaves the Army unable to evade responsibility for administrative failures, which may induce greater prudence.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Despatch No. 2268: Political Developments in Japan, February 1 to 16, 1937
subfiles.to: Wallace T. Treadwell, Eugene H. Dooman, and Stanley K. Hornbeck

subfiles.about: Comprehensive report on the formation of the Hayashi Cabinet, cabinet personnel, budget revisions, factional maneuvering by the Kwantung Army, and plans for a single national party.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 2268 provides an in-depth analysis of the Hayashi Cabinet's lineup and the political maneuvers surrounding its organization between February 1 and 16, 1937. It reveals that Hayashi initially attempted to install Kwantung Army extremist Seishiro Itagaki and Admiral Suetsugu in the Cabinet, but was blocked by Navy moderates who installed Admiral Mitsumasa Yonai and Army leaders who selected Gen Sugiyama. The despatch explains that the Itagaki faction aims for war against the Soviet Union, state socialism, and the creation of an Army-led single party to subdue the Diet, utilizing organizations led by retired officers like Yoshitsugu Tatekawa and Kingoro Hashimoto. An attached clipping from The Japan Advertiser of February 16, 1937, provides Hayashi's speech before the Diet requesting cooperation.
subfiles.title: Political Developments in Japan, February 1 to 16, 1937 (Despatch No. 2268)
